introduction-the-tower-of-babel-problem.core: Without shared names, one service records http.status, another statusCode, a third response_code. Dashboards, alerts and vendor features (service maps, automatic error detection) then can't work across services. OpenTelemetry semantic conventions define standard attribute names, types and meanings for common concepts (HTTP, databases, messaging, cloud, Kubernetes), so telemetry from any service and library means the same thing.

first_principles.problem: A cross-service error dashboard needs a query that checks five different attribute names for HTTP status.
truths: Vendors build features on known names.

analogy.title: The Tower of Babel
analogy.story: Builders speaking different languages can't cooperate; one shared language lets them build together.
analogy.breaks: Languages evolve slowly; conventions version and change.

check.q: Why do vendor features like automatic service maps depend on semantic conventions?
check.a: They recognise standard attribute names (e.g. server.address, db.system) to infer relationships and behaviour.

what-are-semantic-conventions.core: Semantic conventions are versioned specifications in the OpenTelemetry project that define, per domain, span names, attribute names (namespaced like http.request.method or db.operation.name), types, allowed values, requirement levels (required, conditionally required, recommended, opt-in), metric names and units (http.server.request.duration in seconds), and resource attributes. Stability levels (experimental to stable) signal how safe they are to depend on.

first_principles.problem: Engineers invent attribute names for database calls without knowing a standard exists.
truths: Specs define names, types and units.

analogy.title: A building code
analogy.story: It specifies exactly how wiring and plumbing must be labelled and sized, so any electrician can work on any building.
analogy.breaks: Building codes are law; conventions are voluntary but tooling relies on them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every HTTP span looks the same everywhere.

code.text:
span name: GET /api/orders/{id}
http.request.method = "GET"            (required)
url.path = "/api/orders/42"             (required)
http.route = "/api/orders/{id}"        (conditionally required)
http.response.status_code = 200          (conditionally required)
server.address = "shop.example.com"     (recommended)
metric: http.server.request.duration (unit s, histogram)

check.q: What unit do OTel semantic conventions use for HTTP request duration metrics?

resource-attributes-defining-the-who.core: Resource attributes describe the entity producing telemetry, and they apply to every span, metric and log from that process: service.name, service.version, service.namespace, deployment.environment.name, plus detected cloud.provider, cloud.region, host.name, k8s.namespace.name, k8s.pod.name and container.id. They're set once (env vars or resource detectors) and let you filter and group all signals consistently by service, version and location.

first_principles.problem: Traces show 'unknown_service:java' because service.name was never set.

analogy.title: A return address on every envelope
analogy.story: Every letter from the same office carries the same sender details, so replies and sorting work.
analogy.breaks: Return addresses are written once; detectors fill some automatically.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All telemetry grouped by service, version and env.

check.q: What happens if service.name isn't set in OpenTelemetry?
check.a: Telemetry gets a default like unknown_service:<process>, making it hard to group or find.

span-and-metric-attributes-defining-the-.core: Span and metric attributes describe the operation: for HTTP, method, route, status and server address; for databases, db.system.name, db.operation.name, db.collection.name and a sanitised db.query.text; for messaging, messaging.system, destination name and operation; for RPC, rpc.system, service and method. Errors use error.type plus exception events. Metric attributes must stay low-cardinality (route templates, not IDs), while span attributes can be richer.

first_principles.problem: Database spans can't be grouped by table because each team records the query differently.

analogy.title: Labels on a product: category, size, colour
analogy.story: Standard labels let any store sort and count items the same way.
analogy.breaks: Products have few labels; telemetry can have many, which risks cardinality.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Group DB latency by table and operation everywhere.

code.text:
span name: SELECT orders
db.system.name = "postgresql"
db.operation.name = "SELECT"
db.collection.name = "orders"
db.query.text = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1"   (parameterised, no values)
server.address = "orders-db.internal"
error.type = "timeout"   (only on failure)

check.q: Why should metric attributes be more restricted than span attributes?
check.a: Each unique metric attribute combination creates a time series, so high-cardinality values explode storage; spans are individual events.

unified-service-tagging-the-golden-trio.core: Three attributes tie every signal together: service.name (which service), service.version (which release) and deployment.environment.name (prod, staging). Datadog calls them env, service and version unified tagging. Applied consistently to traces, metrics, logs and profiles, they enable filtering any signal by service and environment, comparing versions during deploys, and linking signals seamlessly.

first_principles.problem: Metrics tag service as 'checkout-api', traces as 'checkout', and logs as 'shop-checkout', so nothing links up.

analogy.title: Name, edition and printing of a book
analogy.story: Every review, sales figure and error report cites the same three facts, so they can be combined.
analogy.breaks: Books keep editions; services deploy many versions per day.

check.q: What are the three 'golden trio' attributes?

the-semantic-conventions-package-using-c.core: OTel publishes generated constant packages per language (semconv in Go, opentelemetry-semantic-conventions in Python and Java) containing attribute keys and enum values as code constants. Using semconv.HTTPRouteKey instead of the string 'http.route' prevents typos, gives IDE completion, and makes upgrades visible through compiler or lint errors when names change. Pin the semconv version you emit and set schema_url accordingly.

first_principles.problem: A typo 'http.reponse.status_code' silently breaks an error dashboard for one service.

analogy.title: Using a dropdown instead of a free-text field
analogy.story: You can't misspell an option you pick from a list.
analogy.breaks: Dropdowns are UI; constants need imports and upgrades.

code.text:
import semconv "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.26.0"

span.SetAttributes(
    semconv.HTTPRoute("/api/orders/{id}"),
    semconv.HTTPResponseStatusCode(200),
    semconv.DBSystemPostgreSQL,
)
// resource with schema URL
res := resource.NewWithAttributes(semconv.SchemaURL, semconv.ServiceName("checkout"))

check.q: What does setting schema_url on a resource communicate?
check.a: Which semantic conventions version the telemetry follows, so backends can interpret or translate attribute names.

conventions-evolve-handling-breaking-cha.core: Semantic conventions change. HTTP was stabilised in 2023 with renames (http.method to http.request.method, http.status_code to http.response.status_code, net.peer.name to server.address), and database conventions followed. Instrumentation libraries offer transition modes (OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=http/dup emits both old and new) and Collectors can rename attributes via the schema or transform processors. Migrate dashboards and alerts deliberately.

first_principles.problem: After upgrading instrumentation, all HTTP dashboards go blank because attribute names changed.

analogy.title: Street renaming in a city
analogy.story: For a while signs show both old and new names, until maps and residents catch up.
analogy.breaks: Cities rename rarely; conventions changed several domains in a few years.

code.text:
export OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=http/dup
# Collector transform for legacy senders:
# processors:
#   transform:
#     trace_statements:
#       - context: span
#         statements:
#           - set(attributes["http.request.method"], attributes["http.method"]) where attributes["http.method"] != nil
#           - delete_key(attributes, "http.method")

check.a: Makes instrumentation emit both old and new stable HTTP attribute names during migration.
